newsitem.title: USA: Waxman says documents suggest tobacco fraud.
newsitem.headline: Waxman says documents suggest tobacco fraud.

text.p: A leading anti-smoking lawmaker Thursday released what he called confidential industry documents that he said suggest cigarette makers may have schemed to "defraud and deceive" the public for decades.

Representative Henry Waxman, a California Democrat, made public a handful of the thousands of confidential documents from Liggett and Myers Tobacco Co. he has obtained. He said they showed disturbing patterns of "potentially criminal or fraudulent conduct" by the industry and its lawyers.

A spokesman for the parent company of Liggett, Brooke Group Ltd., declined to comment on the Waxman allegations. A spokesman for the Tobacco Institute, the Washington-based industry group, was not available.

Breaking ranks with other tobacco companies, Liggett in March settled suits with several states and agreed to turn over confidential documents. They have not been made public pending rulings by judges on whether that would violate attorney-client privilege, as other cigarette makers claim.
Waxman said these were not the most crucial Liggett documents and did not include any that describe Liggett's joint defence strategies with other tobacco companies.
He would not say how he got the papers, which date from the 1960s and '70s. A source familiar with the Liggett case said the company in March gave some papers to state officials.

Waxman said that claim of attorney-client privilege was a sham, hiding the involvement of lawyers in what he alleged was "an elaborate scheme to defraud and deceive the American public for over 30 years" by blocking the company from talking about health risks or promoting a "safer" cigarette.
Waxman cited five cases in which judges concluded the confidential documents fall outside the standard privilege.

For instance, in one document lawyers advise against pressing ahead with a safer cigarette, known as the catalyst. If the company presented scientific evidence that the new product was less likely to produce tumours, it would be tantamount to admitting that standard cigarettes did cause tumours, the lawyers said.

"In the case of civil litigation aimed at cancer of the lung, emphysema, heart disease, etc. the running of a catalyst cigarette advertisement making reference specificially or impliedly to reduction in health hazards may incite accelerated cancer litigation which may, in turn, result in infinite liability," the lawyers wrote.
Another document showed attorneys describing their revisions to a letter Liggett had planned to send to physicians. The lawyers said it would "knock the props from under us" in future litigation.
Waxman made the accusations in a news conference and in a report released by the Democratic staff of the House Committee on Government Reform and Oversight.
At least 36 state attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry. Settlement talks have hit a crucial stage, with the first case, in Mississippi, scheduled to go to trial in July.
Republican congressional leaders have warned that time is running out for lawmakers to act on any broad industry settlement, which would need approval from Congress.

One of the fiercest congressional critics of the industry, Waxman said he was making the documents public because if there was a settlement, he wants to ensure broad disclosure about the companies' past activities and require accountability for the sake of public health.

He said he would introduct a Tobacco Accountability Act, which would set up a five-member independent board to monitor industry release of all documents relating to health effects of tobacco, the "manipulation or control" of nicotine, and the sale or marketing of tobacco products to children.

Also Thursday Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat, said he had found a potential "escape hatch" for the tobacco companies embedded in a product liability law recently approved by the Senate Commerce Committee.

He said that even if the tobacco industry fails to get the liability limits it sought in the settlement talks, it could get that protection from the liability law. He said he will introduce an amendment to block it, although he acknowledged that so far no Republicans have joined his effort.
"There is a card up the industry's sleeve," Lautenberg said. "We will fight a bailout for the tobacco industry." He said so far 16 state attorney generals have endorsed his plan.
